code.title: Big-O: counting the steps of a single loop and a double loop

followUps: We drop constants because they depend on the machine and the language, not on the algorithm, and they do not change how the cost grows. A loop doing 3 steps per item costs 3n; on a faster computer it might behave like 1n. Either way, doubling n doubles the time. Compare 100n with n2: at n = 10 the first is larger (1,000 against 100), but from n = 100 onwards n2 is larger for ever (at n = 10,000 it is 100 times larger). Big-O keeps only the part that decides what happens on large inputs. Constants still matter when two algorithms have the same Big-O.

No, O(2n) and O(n) are the same class. Big-O allows any constant multiplier c, so 2n ≤ 2·n proves that 2n is O(n), and n ≤ 2n proves the reverse. Example: two passes over an array of 1,000 items do 2,000 steps, one pass does 1,000; both double when the array doubles, so both are linear. Write O(n), never O(2n). The real difference (one pass is about twice as fast as two) is a constant-factor detail you mention separately. This only applies to multipliers: 2n and n2 are not the same as n.

Every standard library has one of each.

  • O(1): reading an array element or a hash map lookup (average): arr[i], Java HashMap.get, Python d[key], JS Map.get, C++ unordered_map::find, C# Dictionary[key].
  • O(log n): binary search or a balanced-tree or heap operation: Java Arrays.binarySearch, TreeMap.get, PriorityQueue.add; Python bisect.bisect_left, heapq.heappush; C++ lower_bound, map::find.
  • O(n log n): sorting: Java Arrays.sort, Python sorted, JS Array.prototype.sort, C++ std::sort, C# Array.Sort.

For 1,000,000 items that is about 1, 20 and 20,000,000 steps.

code.title: Linear search: best case 1 comparison, worst case n comparisons
code.python:
# Returns how many comparisons were needed to find target (or to give up)
def comparisons(a, target):
    count = 0
    for x in a:
        count += 1          # one comparison per element looked at
        if x == target:     # found: stop early
            break
    return count

a = [7, 3, 9, 4, 8, 1, 5, 2]
print("array = [7, 3, 9, 4, 8, 1, 5, 2]")
# Best case: the target is the first element -> Theta(1)
print("search 7 (first):   " + str(comparisons(a, 7)) + " comparisons")
# Worst case: the target is last or missing -> Theta(n)
print("search 2 (last):    " + str(comparisons(a, 2)) + " comparisons")
print("search 6 (missing): " + str(comparisons(a, 6)) + " comparisons")
# Time: O(n) and Omega(1) over all inputs. Space: O(1).

followUps: Yes, it is true, but it is a loose statement. O is only an upper bound ("grows no faster than"), and merge sort's n log n steps are always below n2: for n = 1,000 it does about 10,000 steps against 1,000,000. So merge sort is O(n2), O(n3) and O(2n) too, in the same way that "I am under 200 years old" is true. The useful statement is the tight one: merge sort is Θ(n log n) in the best, average and worst case. In an interview always give the tightest bound you can prove, and say "O(n2) is true but not tight" if asked.

It is Θ(n). On sorted input each new element is compared once with the element on its left, found to be already in place, and nothing is shifted. For [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] that is 4 comparisons and 0 moves; in general n − 1 comparisons. It cannot be less than about n because every element must be looked at once, so the bound is tight in both directions: O(n) and Ω(n), hence Θ(n). Space is O(1). This best case is why insertion sort is used for small or nearly sorted ranges inside TimSort. The worst case, reversed input, is Θ(n2): n(n−1)/2 comparisons.

code.title: Nested loops: counting inner steps for three common shapes

followUps: The total is O(n log n). For a fixed i, j takes the values 1, 2, 4, 8, … below i, which is about log2 i iterations. Summing over all i gives log 1 + log 2 + … + log n = log(n!), and log(n!) is Θ(n log n). A quick way to see it: half of the i values are at least n/2, and each of those costs at least log(n/2) steps, so the total is at least (n/2)·log(n/2); it is at most n·log n. Check with n = 8: the inner loop runs 0, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3 times for i = 1..8, total 17, close to 8·log28 = 24 (same growth, smaller constant). Space is O(1).

It is O(n) because each pointer only ever moves forward, so together they can move at most 2n times, no matter how the moves are split between the outer and inner loop. Do not multiply the loops; count the total number of pointer moves instead.

int left = 0;
for (int right = 0; right < n; right++) {
    sum += a[right];
    while (sum > k) sum -= a[left++];
}

Here right moves exactly n times. left never goes back and never passes right, so the while body runs at most n times in total over the whole run. For n = 8 that is at most 16 steps, not 64. Time O(n), space O(1). This is an amortised argument.

code.title: log2 n: how many times can n be halved before it reaches 1
code.python:
# Count the halvings needed to bring n down to 1 (this is floor(log2 n))
def halvings(n):
    steps = 0
    while n > 1:
        n //= 2          # throw away half of what is left
        steps += 1
    return steps

# Even a huge n needs only a handful of halvings

values = [8, 1000, 1000000000, 1000000000000000000]
for n in values:
    print("n=" + str(n) + " halvings=" + str(halvings(n)))
# Time: O(log n).
# Space: O(1).

followUps: The base matters as soon as the logarithm sits in an exponent, because then the "constant factor" becomes a different power of n. Example: 2log2 n = n, but 2log4 n = √n. For n = 1,000,000 that is 1,000,000 against 1,000. In the same way nlog2 3 ≈ n1.585 (Karatsuba multiplication) is very different from nlog3 3 = n. Exponential bases differ too: 3n is not O(2n), since 3n/2n = 1.5n grows without limit. Outside an exponent, as in O(n log n), the base is only a constant multiplier and can be dropped. Constants also still matter in real running time: a B-tree with base 100 does far fewer disk reads than a binary tree.

About 30. Each comparison halves the range that can still contain the answer, and 230 = 1,073,741,824 is the first power of two above 109, so after 30 halvings at most one candidate is left. Quick mental method: 103 ≈ 210, so 109 ≈ 230. Compare that with linear search, which may need 1,000,000,000 comparisons. Doubling the data to 2·109 items adds just one more comparison. Time is O(log n) and space is O(1) for the loop version (O(log n) stack for the recursive one). In Java remember that the index type must cope with lo + hi: use lo + (hi - lo) / 2.

code.title: Auxiliary space: reversing with a copy (O(n)) vs in place (O(1))
code.python:
def show(a):
    return "[" + ", ".join(str(x) for x in a) + "]"

a = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
print("input:    " + show(a))
# Version 1: build a new array -> n extra cells, O(n) auxiliary space
copy = [0] * len(a)
for i in range(len(a)):
    copy[i] = a[len(a) - 1 - i]
print("copy:     " + show(copy) + " extra cells = " + str(len(copy)))
# Version 2: swap the two ends and walk inwards -> O(1) auxiliary space
lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
while lo < hi:
    tmp = a[lo]              # the only extra memory: one temp value
    a[lo] = a[hi]
    a[hi] = tmp
    lo += 1
    hi -= 1
print("in place: " + show(a) + " extra cells = 1")
# Time: O(n) for both. Space: O(n) vs O(1).

followUps: No. Recursive Fibonacci takes O(2n) time but only O(n) space. Space counts the frames that are alive at the same moment, not all the calls ever made. The calls run one after another: fib(n) calls fib(n-1), which goes all the way down and returns (freeing its frames) before fib(n-2) starts. So the stack only ever holds one path from the root to a leaf, at most n frames. For fib(30) there are about 1.6 million calls (832,040 of them are leaves), yet never more than 30 frames on the stack. In general: time = number of nodes in the recursion tree, space = its depth.

Merge sort needs O(n) extra space and heap sort needs O(1). Merge sort cannot merge two sorted halves inside the same array easily, so it uses a temporary array of up to n elements, plus O(log n) stack frames for the recursion; n dominates, giving O(n). Heap sort treats the array itself as the heap: it builds a max-heap in place, then repeatedly swaps the root with the last unsorted position and sifts down, using only a few variables. For 1,000,000 ints, merge sort needs about 4 MB of extra memory and heap sort almost none. The trade-off: merge sort is stable and cache-friendly; heap sort is not stable and jumps around in memory. Both run in O(n log n) time.

code.title: Constraints to complexity: which plans fit in 10^8 operations for N = 10^5
code.python:
n = 100000
limit = 100000000          # about 10^8 simple operations per second
log = 0                    # ceil(log2 n)
while (1 << log) < n:
    log += 1
root = 0                   # floor(sqrt n)
while (root + 1) * (root + 1) <= n:
    root += 1
names = ["O(N)", "O(N log N)", "O(N sqrt N)", "O(N^2)"]
ops = [n, n * log, n * root, n * n]   # N^2 = 10^10 would overflow a 32-bit int
print("N=" + str(n) + " log2=" + str(log) + " sqrt=" + str(root) + " budget=" + str(limit))
for i in range(len(names)):
    # A plan is safe when its operation count stays under the budget
    verdict = "fits" if ops[i] <= limit else "too slow"
    print(names[i] + " -> " + str(ops[i]) + " operations: " + verdict)
# Time: O(log n + sqrt n) for this estimate. Space: O(1).

followUps:
Plug N into candidate complexities and keep the largest one that stays near 108 operations.

  • N ≤ 500: O(N3) is fine: 5003 = 1.25·108. Think Floyd–Warshall, interval DP, three nested loops.
  • N ≤ 20: exponential is allowed: 220·20 ≈ 2·107. Think bitmask DP or trying every subset. (20! ≈ 2.4·1018 is far too big; all permutations only work up to about N = 10 or 11.)
  • N ≤ 1018: you cannot even loop to N. Aim for O(log N) (about 60 steps: binary search on the answer, fast exponentiation) or an O(1) formula; O(√N) = 109 is already too slow.

The constraint is a strong hint about the intended technique.

Because "one operation" is not a fixed amount of time. The real speed depends on:

  • The kind of operation: adding two ints takes about a nanosecond; a division, a hash map lookup or a cache miss can take 10 to 100 times longer.
  • The language: C++ and Java manage roughly 108 to 109 simple steps per second; plain Python manages about 107.
  • Hidden constants: an O(N log N) solution with a constant of 50 does more work than the formula suggests.
  • The machine and time limit of the judge.

So treat it as a rough guide: under 107 is safe everywhere, 108 is usually fine in a compiled language with a simple inner loop, and 109 is risky. When you are near the limit, look at the constant.

code.title: Amortised cost: element copies when a dynamic array doubles vs grows by 10
code.python:
# Simulate n appends and count how many elements get copied during resizes
def copies(n, doubling):
    copied = 0
    capacity = 1 if doubling else 10
    size = 0
    for i in range(n):
        if size == capacity:            # full: move everything to a bigger block
            copied += size
            capacity = capacity * 2 if doubling else capacity + 10
        size += 1
    return copied

for n in [1000, 2000, 4000]:
    # Doubling: copies stay below 2n. Plus-10: copies grow like n^2 / 20.
    print("appends=" + str(n) + " doubling copies=" + str(copies(n, True))
          + " plus-10 copies=" + str(copies(n, False)))
# Doubling: O(1) amortised per append. Plus-10: O(n) amortised. Space: O(n).

followUps: Because several keys can land in the same bucket, and in the worst case they all do. A hash map turns the key into a bucket number; with a good hash function and a load factor kept below about 0.75, each bucket holds about one entry, so get looks at one or two entries: O(1) on average. But if many keys collide (a poor hashCode, or keys chosen by an attacker), one bucket holds all n entries and get must search through them: O(n). Example: a hashCode that always returns 42 puts 10,000 keys in one bucket. Java 8+ limits the damage by turning a long bucket into a red-black tree, giving O(log n) worst case when keys are comparable. C++ unordered_map and Python dict stay O(n) in the worst case.

Count the total number of element copies caused by resizes over n appends, then divide by n.

Doubling: resizes happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, …, up to at most n, copying 1 + 2 + 4 + … + n < 2n elements. Add n for the writes themselves: under 3n in total, so at most 3 steps per append, which is O(1) amortised. For n = 1,000 the copies are 1 + 2 + … + 512 = 1,023.

Growing by +10: resizes happen at sizes 10, 20, 30, …, about n/10 of them, copying 10 + 20 + … + n ≈ n2/20 elements. Divided by n that is n/20 per append: O(n) amortised, O(n2) in total. For n = 1,000 the copies are 49,500.

The difference: a geometric series is dominated by its last term, an arithmetic series is not.

code.title: Max-heap: swaps for bottom-up heapify vs inserting one by one
code.python:
# Bottom-up build: sift every non-leaf node down, starting from the last one
def build_bottom_up(h, n):
    swaps = 0
    for start in range(n // 2 - 1, -1, -1):
        i = start
        while True:
            big, l, r = i, 2 * i + 1, 2 * i + 2
            if l < n and h[l] > h[big]:
                big = l
            if r < n and h[r] > h[big]:
                big = r
            if big == i:               # a node moves down at most its height
                break
            h[i], h[big] = h[big], h[i]
            swaps += 1
            i = big
    return swaps

# One-by-one build: each new item is sifted up towards the root
def build_by_insert(h, n):
    swaps = 0
    for size in range(1, n):
        i = size
        while i > 0 and h[(i - 1) // 2] < h[i]:   # up to log n levels per item
            p = (i - 1) // 2
            h[i], h[p] = h[p], h[i]
            swaps += 1
            i = p
    return swaps

for n in [15, 1023, 65535]:
    a = list(range(1, n + 1))          # input 1..n (worst case for insert)
    b = list(range(1, n + 1))
    print("n=" + str(n) + " bottom-up swaps=" + str(build_bottom_up(a, n))
          + " insert swaps=" + str(build_by_insert(b, n)))
# Time: O(n) bottom-up, O(n log n) by insertion. Space: O(1) extra.

followUps:
Anywhere the work shrinks by a constant fraction each round, because n + n/2 + n/4 + … is less than 2n. Common examples:

  • Dynamic array doubling: copies of 1 + 2 + 4 + … + n < 2n over n appends.
  • Quickselect (k-th smallest): each partition keeps on average a fraction of the range, so n + n/2 + n/4 + … = O(n) expected. Median-of-medians makes it O(n) worst case.
  • T(n) = T(n/2) + n recurrences in general, for example "scan, then recurse on one half".
  • Summing a complete binary tree level by level: levels have 1, 2, 4, … nodes, so the last level is half of everything.

For n = 1,024: 1,024 + 512 + … + 1 = 2,047, just under 2n.

The height is ⌊log2 n⌋, counting edges from the root to the deepest node. A heap is a complete binary tree: every level is full except possibly the last, which fills from the left. Level k holds up to 2k nodes, so a tree of height h holds between 2h and 2h+1 − 1 nodes. Examples: n = 1 gives height 0; n = 7 gives height 2 (levels of 1, 2 and 4 nodes); n = 8 gives height 3; n = 1,000,000 gives height 19. This is why push and pop are O(log n): each moves an item along at most one root-to-leaf path. With array storage, the children of index i are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2.

code.title: Deep recursion replaced by a loop with an explicit stack

followUps:
Push a node's children in reverse order, so that the first child is on top of the stack and gets popped first. A stack is last-in first-out, so pushing children left to right would visit them right to left.

stack.push(root);
while (!stack.isEmpty()) {
    Node cur = stack.pop();
    visit(cur);                          // pre-order
    for (int i = cur.kids.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--)
        stack.push(cur.kids.get(i));
}

Example: root 1 with children 2, 3, 4. Push 4, 3, 2; pop 2 first, so the order is 1, 2, 3, 4 as in the recursion. For a graph, mark a node visited when you pop it (and skip it if already marked) to match the recursive order exactly. For post-order work, push (node, state) pairs or keep an iterator per frame. Time O(V + E), space O(V) on the heap.

Because the smaller side has at most half of the elements, so each real recursive call works on a range at most half the size of the one before. Starting from n, the sizes on the stack are at most n/2, n/4, n/8, …, which reaches 1 after log2 n steps. The larger side is not recursed into at all: it is handled by looping, which reuses the current frame.

while (lo < hi) {
    int p = partition(a, lo, hi);
    if (p - lo < hi - p) { sort(a, lo, p - 1); lo = p + 1; }
    else                 { sort(a, p + 1, hi); hi = p - 1; }
}

For n = 1,000,000 the depth is at most 20 frames, even on already-sorted input with a bad pivot, where naive quicksort would go 1,000,000 deep. Only the stack is fixed: the time can still be O(n2) with bad pivots.

code.title: Trial division: steps double for every 2 extra bits of N
code.python:
primes = [97, 10007, 1000003, 1000000007]
for n in primes:
    bits = 0                       # input size = number of binary digits
    t = n
    while t > 0:
        bits += 1
        t //= 2
    steps = 0
    prime = True
    # Try every divisor up to sqrt(n): about 2^(bits/2) steps
    d = 2
    while d * d <= n:
        steps += 1
        if n % d == 0:
            prime = False
            break
        d += 1
    print("N=" + str(n) + " bits=" + str(bits) + " divisions=" + str(steps) + " prime=" + ("yes" if prime else "no"))
# Time: O(sqrt N) = O(2^(b/2)) for a b-bit number, exponential in b. Space: O(1).

followUps: Because W is a number in the input, not the size of the input, and O(n·W) is exponential in the number of bits used to write W. A capacity W takes only b = log2 W bits to write down, so n·W = n·2b. Example: adding 10 bits to W (say from 1,000 to 1,000,000) makes the input 10 bits longer but the DP table 1,000 times bigger. With W = 1018, about 60 bits, the table is impossible. NP-hardness is about running time measured against input length, so there is no contradiction. Such algorithms are called pseudo-polynomial: fast when the numbers are small (W up to about 106), not in general. Problems that stay hard even with small numbers are called strongly NP-hard; knapsack is only weakly NP-hard.

It is polynomial: for b-bit numbers Euclid's algorithm makes O(b) division steps, and the total bit-level cost is O(b2). The number of steps is small because after two steps the larger number has at least halved: a % b is always less than a/2 when b ≤ a. So the loop runs at most about 2·log2 N times (the exact worst case is consecutive Fibonacci numbers, about 1.44·log2 N). Example: gcd(1071, 462) goes 1071, 462, 147, 21, 0, just 3 divisions. For 64-bit values that is under 100 steps, each one machine instruction, so we treat it as O(log N). For huge numbers each division costs up to O(b2), giving the easy bound O(b3); a careful count shows the whole run is O(b2). Unlike O(√N) trial division, this is truly polynomial in the input size.

code.title: Recurrences by counting: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n and T(n) = T(n/2) + n

followUps:
T(n) = T(n−1) + n is Θ(n2), and T(n) = 2T(n−1) + 1 is Θ(2n).

First: unroll it. T(n) = n + (n−1) + (n−2) + … + 1 = n(n+1)/2. For n = 4: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10. It is a chain of n calls where each does a little less work; this is quicksort with the worst pivot or selection sort written recursively.

Second: each call makes two calls on a problem only one smaller, so level k of the tree has 2k calls, each costing 1. Total 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2n−1 = 2n − 1. For n = 4 that is 15. This is the Tower of Hanoi. Note the Master Theorem does not apply to either, because the size shrinks by subtraction, not division. Stack space is O(n) for both.

The recursion itself uses O(log n) stack space; the whole algorithm uses O(n) because of the merge buffer. Each call splits the range in half, so the deepest chain of calls is log2 n frames, and only one chain is alive at a time (the left half finishes and returns before the right half starts). Each frame holds a few integers. For n = 1,000,000 that is about 20 frames. The temporary array used for merging is the big part: up to n elements at the top-level merge. If you allocate a new buffer in every call, the buffers alive at once are n + n/2 + n/4 + … < 2n, still O(n); allocating one buffer once and reusing it is cleaner. Merge sort on a linked list needs no buffer, so there it is O(log n) total.

code.title: Insertion sort (O(n^2)) beats merge sort (O(n log n)) on a small, nearly sorted array
code.python:
cmp = 0                                # comparisons made by the sort being measured

def insertion_sort(a):
    global cmp
    for i in range(1, len(a)):
        key, j = a[i], i - 1
        while j >= 0:
            cmp += 1
            if a[j] <= key:            # already in place: stop after one comparison
                break
            a[j + 1] = a[j]
            j -= 1
        a[j + 1] = key

def merge_sort(a, lo, hi):             # sorts a[lo..hi)
    global cmp
    if hi - lo < 2:
        return
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    merge_sort(a, lo, mid)
    merge_sort(a, mid, hi)
    tmp = []                           # extra memory on every merge
    i, j = lo, mid
    while i < mid and j < hi:
        cmp += 1
        if a[i] <= a[j]:
            tmp.append(a[i]); i += 1
        else:
            tmp.append(a[j]); j += 1
    tmp.extend(a[i:mid])
    tmp.extend(a[j:hi])
    a[lo:hi] = tmp

def measure(label, data):
    global cmp
    x, y = list(data), list(data)
    cmp = 0; insertion_sort(x); ins = cmp
    cmp = 0; merge_sort(y, 0, len(y)); mer = cmp
    print(label + ": insertion=" + str(ins) + " merge=" + str(mer) + " comparisons")

# Small and nearly sorted: the "worse" Big-O does less work
measure("n=8 nearly sorted [1,2,4,3,5,6,8,7]", [1, 2, 4, 3, 5, 6, 8, 7])
# Large and reversed: now the growth rate decides
measure("n=2000 reversed", [2000 - i for i in range(2000)])
# Time: insertion O(n^2) worst, O(n) nearly sorted; merge O(n log n). Space: O(1) vs O(n).

followUps:
Run both on the same realistic inputs, many times, after a warm-up, and compare the middle result, not one run.

  • Same data: generate inputs once with a fixed random seed; test several sizes (for example 102, 104, 106) and shapes (random, sorted, many duplicates).
  • Warm up: in Java and JS the JIT compiles hot code after some runs, so discard the first rounds. Use JMH, timeit, Google Benchmark or BenchmarkDotNet.
  • Repeat: take the median of at least 10 runs and report the spread.
  • Use the result: print or checksum the output, or the compiler may delete the code as unused.
  • Time only the algorithm: build the input outside the timed part, and give each run a fresh copy if the code changes its input.
  • Quiet machine, same build flags, and also measure memory.

Because the insert is only O(1) once you are already standing at the right node, and reaching that node, plus the way nodes are laid out in memory, is slow. Three costs hide behind the O(1):

  • Finding the position is O(n) pointer-following.
  • Cache misses: nodes are scattered over the heap, so each next hop can cost about 100 CPU cycles, while an array is read in order and the processor pre-loads it.
  • Allocation and overhead: every insert allocates a node; a Java LinkedList node for one int costs about 24 bytes plus a boxed Integer, against 4 bytes in an int[].

Shifting 1,000 ints in an array is a single fast memory move, often quicker than walking 1,000 nodes. Lists win only when you already hold the node, as in an LRU cache with a hash map pointing at nodes.

code.title: Hidden O(n*m): 'for each user, check each order' vs one pass with a map
code.python:
users, orders = 1000, 5000
owner = [(i * 7) % users for i in range(orders)]   # order i belongs to this user
print("users=" + str(users) + " orders=" + str(orders))
# Slow: for each user, scan every order -> users * orders checks
slow_work = 0
count_slow = [0] * users
for u in range(users):
    for i in range(orders):
        slow_work += 1
        if owner[i] == u:
            count_slow[u] += 1
# Fast: one pass over the orders, grouping by user in a hash map
fast_work = 0
count_fast = {}
for i in range(orders):
    fast_work += 1
    count_fast[owner[i]] = count_fast.get(owner[i], 0) + 1
same = True
for u in range(users):
    if count_slow[u] != count_fast.get(u, 0):
        same = False
print("nested loops: " + str(slow_work) + " checks")
print("hash map:     " + str(fast_work) + " checks")
print("orders of user 0 = " + str(count_slow[0]) + ", same answers = " + ("yes" if same else "no"))
# Time: O(users * orders) vs O(users + orders). Space: O(users) for the map.

followUps:
Measure how the time grows with the data size, then use a profiler to find the line. Steps:

  1. Reproduce with n, 2n and 4n items. If the time goes up about 4 times per doubling (say 0.5 s, 2 s, 8 s), it is quadratic; about 2 times means linear.
  2. Profile or trace the request and look for a cheap call with a huge call count, or the same SQL query repeated n times (N+1).
  3. Read the hot path for hidden loops: list.contains, indexOf or remove inside a loop; string += in a loop; a nested loop that matches two lists; sorting inside a loop; an ORM lazy load per row.
  4. Fix by building a hash map or set once (O(n)), batching the query with a join or IN, or using a string builder.
  5. Guard it with a test at 10 times the data.

A full scan is fine when n is small and bounded, when the scan is rare or runs offline, or when you need most of the rows anyway. Examples:

  • Small, capped data: a table of 200 countries or 50 feature flags. Scanning 200 rows takes microseconds and an index adds nothing.
  • Low frequency: a nightly report over 107 rows taking 10 seconds is fine; the same scan on every request at 1,000 requests per second is not.
  • You read most rows anyway: exports, aggregates over the whole table. An index does not help if you touch 80% of the rows, and a sequential scan is faster than random index reads.
  • Write-heavy tables where each index slows every insert.

Always ask two things: how often does it run, and can n grow without limit? If n grows with users or time, add a limit, pagination or an index.
